title: Use your records: real profit, safe loans and phone records

say: Use your records: real profit, safe loans, and phone records.
This is the video for Module 4, Using records to grow your business.
Writing records every day is the hard part. Reading them is the rewarding part.
Once a month, ask five questions. Are sales going up or down? Which products make the most money? Is stock going missing? Are debts growing? And is there enough cash to restock?

say: For example, Ifeoma sells household goods in Onitsha. A detergent pack costs her about 1,500 naira and sells for 1,800. That is only 300 naira profit. But she sells about 60 a week, so it earns 18,000 naira.
A bowl set costs 4,000 naira and sells for 6,000, a profit of 2,000 naira. But she sells only about 5 a week, so it earns 10,000.
A fast seller with a small profit can earn more than a slow seller with a big one. So she keeps detergent always in stock.

If you buy goods but sell only part of them, the unsold goods are still on your shelf. So first work out the cost of only what actually left the shop. Opening stock, plus purchases, minus closing stock.

panel.heading: The three profit formulas
items: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases - closing stock
Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold
Net profit = gross profit - running costs

say: Then gross profit is sales minus that cost of goods sold.

panel.heading: The three profit formulas
items: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases - closing stock
Gross profit = sales - cost of goods sold
Net profit = gross profit - running costs

say: Then net profit is gross profit minus running costs, like transport, levy, packaging, phone, staff, charges and bad debts.
Value stock at what you paid, not your selling price. And do not skip the stock count, or your profit can be badly wrong.

panel.rule: Value stock at what you paid. Drawings are not a cost.

say: For example, Halima runs a provisions stall. Her opening stock was worth about 150,000 naira at cost. She bought 520,000 more, and at month end her closing stock was 170,000.
Her sales for October, including credit sales, were about 744,000 naira.
Her cost of goods sold is 150,000 plus 520,000 minus 170,000. That is 500,000 naira. So her gross profit is 244,000.
Her running costs, including one bad debt, were 78,000 naira.
So her net profit is about 166,000 naira. She drew 80,000 for the household, so about 86,000 stayed in the business as extra capital.
Lenders want to see that your business is real, steady and able to pay. Your records answer that. But check for yourself first. Repayments must come from profit, not from capital.
For example, Esther's drinks business makes about 120,000 naira net profit a month.

panel.heading: Can Esther afford this loan?
items: Net profit: about 120,000 naira a month
Household drawing: 80,000 naira
Left after drawing: 40,000 naira
Loan repayment: 55,000 naira
Short by 15,000 naira every month

say: She draws 80,000 for the household, so 40,000 is left.

say: Keep your notebook as the original record, and let the phone do the adding. Install Google Sheets, sign in, and type five headings in row 1.

panel.heading: A cash book in Google Sheets
items: Create a sheet and sign in with Gmail
Headings: Date, Details, Money in, Money out, Balance
Type the opening balance in E2
In E3 type =E2+C3-D3 and copy it down
Check the last balance against your cash

say: Type your opening balance in cell E2. In E3, type equals E2 plus C3 minus D3, and copy it down. The spreadsheet adds for you.
